winners.premise: A pregnant woman notices that several expensive baby-shower gifts are marked purchased on her registry but never arrive, then discovers her sister has been intercepting the deliveries and returning them for store credit before the shower.
winners.conflict: The sister insists the registry is glitching and accuses the narrator of obsessing over gifts, while more purchased items vanish and relatives begin asking why their presents were never acknowledged.
winners.twist: A store employee calls about repeated no-receipt returns tied to the narrator's registry, and security footage shows the sister returning unopened gifts that relatives had shipped to the narrator's home.
winners.hook: Three days before my baby shower, the store called to ask why I had already returned half my gifts.
winners.narration:
I thought the call was a mistake because I had not returned anything. In fact, that was the problem. My registry showed a stroller, bottle sterilizer, baby monitor, diaper bag, and several smaller items as purchased, but none of them had reached me.

At first I assumed relatives had bought the gifts early and planned to bring them to the shower. Then my aunt texted to ask whether I liked the diaper bag she had shipped directly to my apartment two weeks earlier. I told her it had never arrived. She sent me the delivery confirmation. It had been left outside my door while I was at work.

My sister had a spare key because she had been helping me prepare the nursery. When I asked whether she had seen a package that day, she immediately said no and told me pregnancy brain was making me overthink everything. She even joked that I was becoming a detective over gifts I technically was not supposed to open yet.

That explanation almost worked until my college friend called about the baby monitor. She had also shipped it directly to me, and tracking showed it was delivered on a Saturday morning. I was home that entire day, but I remembered my sister arriving early with coffee and insisting I take a nap while she organized the living room.

I checked my building camera. The hallway footage only kept seven days, so the older deliveries were gone. But I could see one recent package arrive at my door at 10:14 in the morning. Twenty minutes later, my sister walked out carrying a large shopping bag I had not noticed when she came in.

I called her again. This time she got angry. She said she had returned one duplicate item because she was trying to help and planned to use the credit to buy something I actually needed. I asked what duplicate item, because I had never received the original. She stopped answering.

The next morning, the baby store called. Their loss-prevention team had flagged several returns connected to my registry. The employee explained that someone had been bringing back unopened products without gift receipts and accepting store credit. Because the registry number had been used to verify the items, the returns were all linked to my account.

I asked whether they could tell who made them. They could not give me the footage directly, but they asked me to come in and confirm whether I recognized the customer. I went with my husband.

On the screen was my sister.

She returned my aunt's diaper bag. Then the sterilizer. Then the baby monitor. In one clip, she was wearing the same jacket she wore to dinner with us that night. She had been collecting the packages from my doorstep or moving them inside with her spare key, then returning them before I even knew they had arrived.

When I confronted her, she finally admitted it. She was behind on credit-card payments and had discovered that registry gifts were easy to return for store credit. She had used some of the credit for groceries and sold the rest through local marketplace groups for cash.

What hurt most was not the money. It was realizing she had let me question my friends, my relatives, the delivery drivers, and even my own memory while she kept telling me I was being dramatic.

I changed the lock that afternoon. Then I called every person whose gift had disappeared and explained what happened before my sister could invent another version.

She told our family I humiliated her over baby supplies.

I told her, "You weren't returning my gifts. You were returning everyone else's trust in you."

The store restored what credit it could, and several relatives replaced their gifts even though I begged them not to. My aunt said the only thing she wanted replaced was the spare key.

For once, everyone agreed.
winners.title: My Sister Returned My Baby Shower Gifts Before I Opened Them
winners.description: My baby registry said the gifts were purchased, but they kept disappearing before I ever saw them. Then the store called about the returns.
winners.payoff: You weren't returning my gifts. You were returning everyone else's trust in you.
